sections.text_content:
USPSTF Clinician Summary of USPSTF Recommendation
Screening for Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults
June 2023

sections.section_name: What does the USPSTF recommend
sections.text_content:
What does the USPSTF recommend?
B
Grade
Adults, including pregnant and postpartum persons, and older adults (65 years or older):
Screen for major depressive disorder (MDD).
I
Statement
Adults, including pregnant and postpartum persons, and older adults (65 years or older):
The evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for suicide risk.

sections.section_name: To whom does this recommendation apply
sections.text_content:
To whom does this recommendation apply?
This recommendation applies to adults (19 years or older), pregnant and postpartum persons, and older adults
(65 years or older) who do not have a diagnosed mental health disorder and are not showing recognized signs or
symptoms of depression or suicide risk.

sections.section_name: What's new
sections.text_content:
What's new?
This recommendation is consistent with the 2014 USPSTF recommendation statement on screening for suicide risk
in adults and older adults and the 2016 recommendation statement on screening for MDD in adults.

sections.section_name: How to implement this recommendation
sections.text_content:
How to implement this recommendation?
• Treatment for MDD in adults includes psychotherapy or pharmacotherapy. Collaborative care is a
multicomponent, health care system–level intervention that uses care managers to link primary care clinicians,
patients, and mental health specialists to ensure patients receive the best care. Clinicians should be aware of the
risk factors, signs, and symptoms of depression and suicide; listen to any patient concerns; and make sure that
persons who need help get it.

sections.section_name: How to implement this recommendation (Part 2)
sections.text_content:
• To achieve the benefit of depression screening and reduce disparities in depression-associated morbidity, it is
important that persons who screen positive are evaluated further for diagnosis and, if appropriate, are provided or
referred for evidence-based care.

sections.section_name: How to implement this recommendation (Part 3)
sections.text_content:
• Clinicians are encouraged to consider the unique balance of benefits and harms in the perinatal period when
deciding the best treatment for depression for a pregnant or breastfeeding person.

sections.section_name: How to implement this recommendation (Part 4)
sections.text_content:
• The USPSTF found no evidence on the optimal frequency of screening for depression. In the absence of evidence,
a pragmatic approach might include screening adults who have not been screened previously and using clinical
judgment while considering risk factors, comorbid conditions, and life events to determine if additional screening
of patients at increased risk is warranted. Ongoing assessment of risks that may develop during pregnancy and
the postpartum period is also a reasonable approach.

sections.section_name: What additional information should clinicians know about this recommendation
sections.text_content: What additional information should clinicians know about this recommendation?

sections.section_name: What additional information should clinicians know about this recommendation (Part 2)
sections.text_content:
• The USPSTF recommends screening for depression in all adults regardless of risk factors. However, there are
some factors that increase risk. These include family history of depression, prior episodes of depression or other
mental health conditions, a history of trauma or adverse life events, or a history of disease or illness.

sections.section_name: What additional information should clinicians know about this recommendation (Part 3)
sections.text_content:
• Risk factors for perinatal depression include life stress, low social support, history of depression, marital or
partner dissatisfaction, and a history of abuse.

sections.section_name: What additional information should clinicians know about this recommendation (Part 4)
sections.text_content:
• Women, young adults, multiracial individuals, and Native American/Alaska Native individuals have higher rates
of depression.

sections.section_name: What additional information should clinicians know about this recommendation (Part 5)
sections.text_content:
• Anxiety and depressive disorders often overlap.
• In the absence of evidence, health care professionals should use their judgement, based on individual patient
circumstances, when determining whether to screen for suicide risk in adults not showing signs or symptoms.

sections.section_name: Why is this recommendation and topic important
sections.text_content:
Why is this recommendation and topic important?
MDD is a common disorder in the US that can have a substantial impact on an individual's life. Depression is
common in postpartum and pregnant persons and affects both the birthing parent and infant. Suicide is the
10th-leading cause of death in US adults.

sections.section_name: What are other relevant USPSTF recommendations
sections.text_content:
What are other relevant USPSTF recommendations?
• Screening for anxiety disorders in adults

sections.section_name: What are other relevant USPSTF recommendations (Part 2)
sections.text_content: • Preventive counseling interventions for perinatal depression

sections.section_name: What are other relevant USPSTF recommendations (Part 3)
sections.text_content:
• Information on additional mental health recommendations for adults from the USPSTF are available at
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/

sections.section_name: What are additional tools and resources
sections.text_content:
What are additional tools and resources?
• The Community Preventive Services Task Force recommends:

sections.section_name: What are additional tools and resources (Part 2)
sections.text_content: - Home-based depression care and depression care management in primary care clinics for older adults

sections.section_name: What are additional tools and resources (Part 3)
sections.text_content: - Collaborative care for the management of depressive disorders

sections.section_name: What are additional tools and resources (Part 4)
sections.text_content:
- Mental health benefits legislation to increase appropriate utilization of mental health services for persons
with mental health conditions

sections.section_name: What are additional tools and resources (Part 5)
sections.text_content:
• The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration maintains a national registry of evidence-
based programs and practices for substance abuse and mental health interventions

sections.section_name: What are additional tools and resources (Part 6)
sections.text_content: • Perinatal Psychiatry Access Programs aim to increase access to perinatal mental health care

sections.section_name: What are additional tools and resources (Part 7)
sections.text_content:
• The Suicide Prevention Resource Center, supported by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services
Administration, offers various resources on suicide prevention

sections.section_name: Where to read the full recommendation statement
sections.text_content:
Where to read the full recommendation statement?
Visit the USPSTF website or the JAMA website to read the full recommendation statement. This includes more
details on the rationale of the recommendation, including benefits and harms; supporting evidence; and recom-
mendations of others.
